A1.justification: Despite the revised title, both PDFs describe PermuCATE for variable importance in CATE estimation. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original LD, HL, and HP simulation results, including importance estimates, statistical power, and estimation-error analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original simulations and additional semi-synthetic IHDP evaluations, including experiments with grouped covariates.

M1.justification: The residual-permutation algorithm remains central. v2 reverses the written risk difference in Algorithm 1 and Equation (4), introduces conditional sampling from logistic-regression probabilities for binary covariates, and evaluates group-level importance, which v1 treated as future work. These are limited corrections and adaptations.

E1.justification: v2 retains LD, HL, and HP and adds IHDP: 747 subjects with 25 real continuous/binary covariates and simulated outcomes. Appendix A.12 additionally evaluates noisy copies of IHDP variables, introducing strongly correlated inputs and group-importance tasks absent from v1.

E2.justification: LOCO remains the single-variable importance comparator. The new grouped experiment evaluates its leave-one-group-out adaptation, LOGO, in Figure 8 alongside grouped PermuCATE in Figure 7. Causal Forest, CATENet, and TabPFN serve as shared underlying CATE learners.

E3.justification: v2 adds HL/HP variance comparisons across Ridge, CATENet, and TabPFN, plus single-train/test-split IHDP evaluations using PEHE and importance-ranking AUC. Group experiments introduce noisy-copy construction and group-based error/power definitions. The original nested five-fold, 80/20 splitting and 50 permutations remain; renaming TP accuracy as power preserves that metric.

E4.justification: New Figure 2 investigates model misspecification and learner-dependent variance; Appendix A.12 tests grouping under redundant, correlated inputs. The dedicated dimensionality-versus-refitting-error analysis in v1 Figure 5 is removed. The feasible-risk comparison is retained, and the earlier LD variance diagnostic moves from Figure 2 to Figure 6.

E5.justification: The LD experiment explicitly increases repetitions from 10 to 100 random samples and replaces the described Wald statistic with the Nadeau–Bengio corrected t-test. New Figure 2 reports bootstrap uncertainty for variance across 100 simulations. Figure 3 still specifies 10 simulations, so the repetition increase is not universal.

E6.justification: The LD importance/detection curves and HL/HP power curves change, alongside new learner-variance, IHDP, and grouping results. Figure 4 newly reports better importance AUC and power for PermuCATE across three learners, with LOCO/CATENet type-I error around 0.08, exceeding 0.05. These additions and revised estimates do not establish same-setting gains between versions; the LD statistical procedure also changed.

T1.justification: v2 adds Assumption 3.1 and Propositions 3.2, 3.4, and 3.5, with Sobol-index consistency and finite-sample error arguments in Appendices A.3–A.8. Training-conditional variance expressions with correlated Gaussian covariates replace v1's uncorrelated linear formulas. It also restores the missing treatment-minus-propensity factor in Equation (S1). However, the new propositions and proofs use normalization inconsistent with Equation (4).

C1.justification: The central claims of model-agnostic importance estimation, lower variance, and higher power remain. v2 promotes the advantage with complex deep-learning estimators from v1's proposed future investigation to an explicitly demonstrated contribution, extending the asserted empirical applicability to real-world covariates.

C2.justification: v2 newly argues that PermuCATE's finite-sample error excludes CATE-estimation error and interprets IHDP LOCO/CATENet failures through stochastic optimization. It explicitly limits high-dimensional coverage to a few hundred covariates after dimensionality reduction. Several former limitations concerning nonlinear theory, semi-synthetic validation, and grouping are replaced by claims and interpretations based on the new analyses.

D1.justification: v2 adds IHDP outcome-generation details, noisy-copy construction with binary flips at probability 0.1, a 100-tree Causal Forest setting, and references to CATENet parameter choices. It explicitly describes nested hyperparameter cross-validation. The original linear and boosting hyperparameter ranges remain essentially unchanged.

R1.justification: The CPI-versus-LOCO positioning remains. v2 adds discussion of attribution methods through Crabbé et al., connects the theory to Sobol and Reyero Lobo et al., and cites the added learners, benchmark, and corrected test. Several earlier references disappear, including Gao, Liu, Dorie, and Shimoni, without replacing the central research framing.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, theoretical narrative, and limitations are substantially rewritten. Experiments are reorganized, the appendix becomes a numbered hierarchy, and an Impact Statement is added. The title and author list also change. These revisions extend beyond prose accompanying new results.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different document layout and redraws Figures 1 and 3 with revised axes, legends, and captions. It adds four multipanel figures, relocates the earlier LD diagnostic to supplementary Figure 6, and removes v1 Figure 5. The feasible-risk plot is retained as Figure 5.

improvement.justification: IHDP, neural/foundation-model, and grouping experiments address important gaps in v1's simulation-based validation; the revised LD inference also adds repetitions and a corrected test. However, the new central theory has conflicting factors of two between Algorithm 1/Equation (4) and the propositions. Appendix A.4 additionally drops cross terms using zero-mean and independent-optimization assumptions absent from Proposition 3.4. These problems affect the stronger finite-sample claims, preventing a reliable net quality judgment despite the empirical benefits.
